title: Deployments as Controlled Experiments

sections.title: Restoration After a Candidate Has Served Traffic
Applying Release Gates to Read Routing

html:
You have probably reviewed a change that seemed safe because the code was small, the tests passed, and the benchmark showed an improvement. The next step is usually familiar. The change is merged, a build is created, and the deployment replaces the running instances. If everything starts and the health checks pass, the release appears to be progressing normally.

Baodium’s Recommendation Service team followed that routine after an engineer rewrote a database query. The new query returned the same recommendations and finished faster in an isolated benchmark. Its functional tests passed, and the team deployed it through a Kubernetes rolling update. There was no new feature for customers to see, so the release attracted little attention at first.

Under concurrent production traffic, however, the new access path performed more database work than the isolated test had exposed. The average time a request occupied a connection rose from 70 to 85 milliseconds. At roughly 400 lookups per second per instance, that increased average connection occupancy from 28 to 34 of the 40 available connections. Bursts filled the remaining slots, acquisition waits increased, and product pages began slowing down again.

Kubernetes continued reporting the new instances as ready. They had started successfully and could answer health requests. The rolling update advanced because nothing in its deployment policy compared connection occupancy or customer latency against the previous version. By the time the team identified the change, much of the fleet was running it.

The engineers restored the earlier image. They then reproduced the regression with representative query parameters and concurrent requests. The database had chosen an access path that looked efficient for one query but caused more contention under the production workload. That distinction had been missing from the release test.

We have spent the previous chapters estimating demand, limiting shared resources, and measuring customer outcomes. A deployment can change all three without changing an API response. This chapter follows the controls Baodium introduced so a new version would have to demonstrate acceptable behavior before reaching the rest of the fleet.

What the Release Must Demonstrate

The first change to the release process was surprisingly small. Before deploying a candidate, the owner recorded what was expected to improve and which observation would cause the release to stop.

For the recommendation query, the expectation was lower query cost under representative traffic. The condition for stopping was increased connection occupancy or acquisition delay, even if isolated SQL execution remained fast. The team also watched recommendation inclusion, product-page latency, and errors, because a resource improvement would be of little value if customers received fewer recommendations or slower pages.

This made the release review more useful than a generic check that all containers were healthy. The engineers knew which measurement the code could affect and how that change would reach customers. If a query held a connection for another 15 milliseconds at 400 lookups per second, it would occupy six additional connections on average in each affected instance. That was a substantial change against a pool limited to forty.

Other releases require different evidence. A new cache namespace needs cache-miss and source-read measurements. A configuration change may require proof that instances have loaded the intended revision. A new background consumer needs evidence about processing rate, duplicate effects, and backlog growth. A library upgrade may need a longer observation period for memory retention.

The release plan is useful when it identifies the specific consequence of the change and the signal that will detect it. Baodium used those signals to select its deployment strategy and determine how much exposure it could allow before making another decision.

Deploying Code and Exposing Behavior

A service can start running a new binary before customers begin using a new feature. The team can deploy both code paths with the new one disabled, verify that the application starts, and then enable the new path for selected requests. Alternatively, it can run old and new binaries at the same time and direct a measured share of traffic to each.

Both approaches give the team more information before full exposure, but they reverse different things. A routing change can stop new traffic from reaching candidate instances. A feature flag can stop a particular path inside a running instance. Neither operation undoes database writes or external actions already performed.

Rolling Updates

The failed release had used an ordinary rolling update. With a suitable maxSurge and maxUnavailable policy, Kubernetes can start replacement Pods, wait for readiness, and remove older Pods progressively. Figure Figure shows the sequence.

Readiness answers whether a particular instance is prepared to receive traffic under its health contract. It cannot establish whether the new version will consume more database connections when thousands of requests arrive. A Deployment’s progress deadline can identify a stalled rollout, but a failed progress check does not automatically restore the previous application version. A release controller or operator must make that decision.

The rollout also needs spare capacity. A terminating Pod may continue processing requests while its replacement becomes ready, so the actual resource demand can exceed the desired replica count plus the configured surge. Chapter 6 examined the effect on database pools. The release plan must include the connections and background work that can continue during termination.

Blue-Green Environments

Baodium also considered maintaining two environments. Blue would serve customers while the new image and configuration were prepared in green. The team could then change traffic routing to green and, if necessary, return new requests to blue.

This can shorten restoration because the earlier environment is already running. It comes with a capacity cost. Both environments may establish database connections, fill caches, run scheduled jobs, or consume external provider allowances. Only the environment with the appropriate authority should execute a singleton task such as a settlement scheduler.

There is also a compatibility condition. If green changes the database so that blue can no longer read or update it, restoring traffic to blue will not restore the service. The rollback target must be tested against the state that the candidate may have produced, a problem we will return to when discussing schema migrations.

Field note

Cloudflare, July 2019

On July 2, 2019, Cloudflare deployed a web application firewall rule containing a regular expression that caused excessive backtracking. The resulting CPU consumption affected requests across its network, producing widespread HTTP errors for approximately 27 minutes.

The rule reached the network within seconds. Cloudflare’s published investigation explained that the normal staged deployment safeguards for software had not applied to this category of rule change. The recovery also depended on a procedure for disabling managed firewall rules during a network-wide incident.

A configuration rule can execute expensive code and change production resource demand just as an application binary can. Baodium consequently applied exposure gates to executable configuration and feature activation, not only container images.

Source: Cloudflare’s published incident analysis.

Choosing a Representative Canary

For the corrected recommendation query, Baodium selected a canary. A small share of production requests would reach the candidate while the stable version continued serving the rest. Engineers could compare the two under similar conditions before approving another increase in exposure.

The fleet normally had twenty Recommendation Service instances, each handling approximately 400 lookups per second, for about 8,000 lookups per second in total. Five percent of that traffic is 400 lookups per second. If the router directs those requests to one canary instance, the candidate sees approximately the same load as a normal stable instance.

Now imagine keeping the traffic weight at five percent but running five canary instances. Each receives only about 80 lookups per second. The query might appear healthy under that load even though the original regression occurred near 400 lookups per second per instance. The release owner therefore needed to choose the number of canary instances and the traffic weight together.

A fifteen-percent stage with three canary instances would again provide about 400 lookups per second to each candidate instance. The router’s actual traffic distribution still had to be measured. Weighted routing cannot guarantee an even request mix or identical rates on every Pod.

Comparing Equivalent Requests

The engineers matched more than request volume. Product category, query parameters, catalog size, region, and cache warmth could all change connection occupancy. A candidate serving mostly small catalogs could look better than a stable instance serving large ones.

The release dashboard therefore showed the request mix and per-instance rate alongside the resource measurements. The team used live production traffic for the comparison. Internal employee traffic remained useful for functional checks, but it could not establish how the new query behaved under the production mix.

The stable and canary populations also needed deliberate scaling. With some progressive-delivery controllers, the stable ReplicaSet keeps all of its original replicas during the canary so an abort can immediately return traffic to a full-size stable fleet. If the stable version keeps twenty instances while one canary receives five percent of traffic, each stable instance receives roughly 380 lookups per second. The canary receives about 400. That difference is small but should be visible in the comparison.

Baodium’s example rollout uses dynamic stable scaling so its planned five-percent stage has one canary and approximately nineteen stable instances. The fifteen-percent stage has three canaries and approximately seventeen stable instances. This keeps normal per-instance load more comparable, but an abort may require scaling the stable fleet back up. The team tested that recovery cost before choosing the policy.

Warm-Up and Shared Dependencies

A new instance starts with empty local caches and freshly established connections. Its first requests may take longer than those served by an instance that has been running all day. The engineers measured this period separately and admitted the candidate to its normal load only after its required initialization and bounded warm-up had completed.

They did not hide startup failures by discarding every early measurement. An instance that takes too long to become usable is itself a release problem. Warm-up duration, source-read spikes, and connection creation belonged in the deployment evidence.

The more difficult limitation was the shared PostgreSQL database. If a canary query increases contention in the shared database, stable requests may slow down too. Comparing only the relative latency between the two versions could then conceal a harmful change because both populations have deteriorated.

Baodium checked absolute database acquisition time and product-page latency alongside the canary-versus-stable comparison. The five-percent traffic weight limited direct exposure to the candidate, but it did not limit the effect of that candidate on every caller sharing PostgreSQL.

Shadow traffic required a similar check. Sending copies of production reads to the candidate can test more request patterns without returning its results to customers. Those copied reads still consume database and cache capacity, so the team gave shadow traffic its own budget. Requests that change business state cannot simply be replayed against production without a plan to prevent additional effects.

Decision review

Promote the recommendation canary?

One canary instance receives approximately 400 lookups per second. After twenty minutes, product-page p99 is 231 ms, compared with 220 ms for the stable population. No correctness errors have been recorded. Mean connection occupancy is 74 ms on the canary and 70 ms on comparable stable instances. The next planned stage is 15 percent exposure.

Promote immediately because the difference in page latency is small.

Pause, verify the recorded release gates and request mix, then promote only if the stage has passed.

Abort because any increase in mean connection occupancy is unacceptable.

The second choice preserves the release policy. At 400 lookups per second, the 4 ms occupancy increase corresponds to about 1.6 more connections assigned on average to the canary. If the same increase appeared on twenty instances, it would add about 32 assigned connections across the fleet under comparable traffic. That estimate does not include secondary contention at greater exposure.

The policy in the next section permits up to a 5 ms mean occupancy increase, so a consistent 4 ms difference can pass after the required samples and absolute checks are verified. That supports promotion to the next measured stage, subject to its planned capacity and risk limits. A small page-latency difference alone is insufficient evidence, while a zero-tolerance occupancy rule would reject changes that the team had already determined the database could accommodate.

Release Gates and Observation Windows

The failed rolling update had no recorded condition for stopping before another instance was replaced. Baodium made those conditions part of the release record. The owner could still investigate an unusual result, but a candidate could not advance merely because someone felt the difference was probably harmless.

The release controller had three possible decisions. It could promote when all required evidence was present and the measurements passed. It could pause when the sample was insufficient or a measurement was missing. It could abort when an explicit correctness or resource threshold failed. Pausing was not a safe response to a confirmed harmful release, since it would leave the affected canary population exposed.

The Recommendation Release Policy

The team began with five percent exposure and one canary instance. It required two passing, nonoverlapping five-minute observations, with at least 50,000 completed lookups on the canary in each interval. At the expected 400 lookups per second, five minutes would produce roughly 120,000 completions, so the minimum also allowed for traffic variation.

initial_exposure:
  traffic_percent: 5
  canary_instances: 1
  expected_lookups_per_instance_per_second: 400

evaluation:
  window_minutes: 5
  passing_nonoverlapping_windows: 2
  min_canary_completions_per_window: 50000

limits:
  mean_connection_occupancy_delta_ms: 5
  connection_acquisition_p99_ms: 20
  incorrect_recommendation_result: abort
  user_facing_regression: abort

missing_evidence:
  action: pause
  maximum_blind_interval_seconds: 60
  after_timeout: abort

restoration:
  target: approved_compatible_stable_release

The occupancy threshold was based on normal variation and the additional connections the database could tolerate under representative load. An increase of 5 ms at 400 lookups per second corresponds to two additional assigned connections per instance on average. The team would not copy that threshold to a service with a different pool size or workload.

Connection-acquisition p99 provided an absolute limit. Even if the candidate and stable populations had similar occupancy, neither should be promoted while the shared database was already causing unacceptable waits. The user-facing checks watched page latency, recommendation inclusion, and correctness, using the outcome definitions from Chapter 8.

An incorrect recommendation result or a confirmed serious customer-facing regression triggered an immediate abort. Missing telemetry prevented promotion. If a required signal did not recover within the defined blind interval, the controller restored stable routing rather than continuing the canary without evidence.

Deriving a Useful Sample

Five-minute intervals were a starting point for this query release because connection occupancy responds quickly to changes in concurrent load. Other risks need longer observation. A memory leak may take hours to become measurable. A scheduled task may run once a day. A cache expiry problem cannot be tested by watching an instance that never reaches its expiry interval.

The team also needed to avoid claiming statistical certainty from a large request count alone. At 400 lookups per second, twenty minutes provides approximately 480,000 lookups. That is substantial evidence about mean connection occupancy, but successive requests are correlated through shared caches and database load. A rare failure that occurs once in a million requests may not appear at all. Such risks need targeted tests and longer observation, not simply a convenient canary duration.

The two evaluation windows were nonoverlapping because repeatedly querying a rolling five-minute window every minute would reuse most of the same requests. A passing result from those overlapping samples would add much less evidence than two separate intervals. Even separate time windows may share the same traffic patterns, so the release owner still examined the request mix and resource conditions.

Recording the Decision

Every stage recorded the image digest, configuration revision, traffic weight, actual canary and stable instance counts, observed request rates, evaluation interval, measured results, and decision. The dashboard used version-specific metrics and aggregated histogram buckets rather than averaging instance percentiles.

Completed-request latency appeared alongside attempts and refusals. A new version that rejected more expensive requests could otherwise look faster simply because fewer difficult operations reached completion. The release owner also tracked shared database capacity so a relative improvement could not conceal deterioration affecting every version.

Automating Promotion With Argo Rollouts

An engineer could compare the measurements by hand, but the team wanted the same gates applied during every release. A progressive-delivery controller such as Argo Rollouts or Flagger can direct traffic through stages and run metric analysis before promotion.

The following Argo Rollout excerpt assumes an Istio traffic router and Service resources for the stable and canary versions. The full resource also needs its ordinary Pod selector and template.

The first stage pairs one canary instance with five percent of traffic. The second pairs three instances with fifteen percent. Dynamic stable scaling reduces the stable ReplicaSet as exposure increases, so the release must reserve enough capacity to restore stable replicas if an abort occurs. The route weight and actual per-instance request rates are verified in production rather than assumed from this YAML alone.

An analysis template queries Prometheus for the measurements used in the release gate. The example below checks the canary sample and the difference between canary and stable mean connection occupancy.

The two measurements run after an initial five-minute observation period and repeat at five-minute intervals. The queries assume that every connection occupancy observation has a reliable rollout-role label, that the populations are comparable, and that neither series has an empty denominator. They compare means computed from the recorded occupancy histogram sums and counts.

This excerpt does not implement the complete policy. Acquisition p99, request outcomes, missing-series handling, and the one-minute blindness watchdog need additional analysis and controller behavior. Argo Rollouts can treat inconclusive analysis as a pause and failed analysis as a reason to abort, but the exact missing-data and error thresholds must be tested in the installed controller version.

The benefit of automation is consistency. The team still chooses which measurements matter and what a safe deviation looks like. The controller applies those decisions every time instead of relying on an engineer to remember them during an evening deployment.

Promoting Through Several Exposure Stages

A passing five-percent canary was useful evidence, though it did not establish that all twenty instances could run the new query safely. At full exposure, the new query would generate far more aggregate database activity. Some effects, such as shared lock contention or cache misses, may increase disproportionately as the candidate takes a larger share.

Baodium advanced through intermediate stages, measuring the request mix and per-instance load at each one. At fifteen percent, three candidate instances each received approximately 400 lookups per second under the assumed fleet rate. The absolute database checks ran again because the shared-resource load was now larger.

The release owner estimated how much additional occupancy the next stage would contribute before approving it. For example, a sustained increase of 4 ms per lookup at 400 lookups per second adds about 1.6 assigned connections on each candidate instance. Across twenty instances the corresponding first-order estimate is 32 additional assigned connections. It remains an estimate because query duration and routing may change as contention rises.

Restoration also becomes more expensive at later stages. When one instance uses the candidate, most serving capacity already runs the stable version. Near full exposure, returning to stable may require starting or replacing many instances. The controller’s routing change is only the first step. The team measured how long healthy stable capacity took to become available and how the database behaved during that transition.

After the final promotion, there was no stable production population left for a simultaneous comparison. The release continued through an observation period using absolute SLO and dependency limits, per-request-class measurements, and the earlier stage evidence.

Feature Flags and Runtime Activation

The recommendation incident had involved a new query implementation, but the same application could have carried both query paths behind a feature flag. The new code could be deployed with the flag disabled, allowing the team to verify startup and compatibility before enabling its production behavior.

A feature-management system such as LaunchDarkly or Unleash can deliver flag configuration to applications. OpenFeature provides an interface for applications using different flag providers. The selected path must be recorded in request telemetry so the team can compare the two implementations even when they run in the same binary.

recommendations_enabled: true
recommendations_exposure_percent: 1
recommendations_revision: 17

The application can assign a customer to a stable cohort by hashing a flag name and customer ID. The simplified implementation below accepts a percentage from zero to one hundred.

The same customer is assigned consistently while the cohort algorithm and flag identity remain unchanged. One percent of customers may generate more than one percent of requests, so the release dashboard still needs the measured request rate and resource consumption. A feature flag is also no substitute for authorization. A customer selected by the flag cannot perform an operation that the business policy forbids.

When the release owner sets exposure to zero, instances must receive and apply the new revision. A disconnected instance may continue using an older cached configuration, and requests already running on the candidate path may continue after the flag is disabled. The rollback procedure therefore checks configuration revisions and actual path selection rather than treating a control-plane acknowledgment as proof of recovery.

Flags need a lifecycle. Once the change is stable and the rollback period has ended, the team removes the old implementation in a separate release and retires the activation flag when no deployed version requires it. Permanent operational switches need assigned owners and periodic tests of the behavior they control.

Field note

Knight Capital, August 2012

Knight Capital deployed new trading software to eight servers before the August 1, 2012 market opening. The new code reached seven servers, while the eighth continued running an older implementation. A flag repurposed for the new function still activated obsolete Power Peg behavior on that server.

The mismatch caused the routing system to send millions of unintended orders into the market. According to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, the incident produced more than four million executions in approximately 45 minutes and ultimately cost Knight more than $460 million.

During the incident, engineers removed the new code from the seven updated servers. That exposed the old behavior on those servers as well and made the situation worse. The deployment had not been verified uniformly across targets, and the restoration procedure had not been tested against the obsolete flag behavior.

The case illustrates why verifying every deployed target, removing retired activation paths, and rehearsing restoration matter as much as delivering the correct source revision.

Source: SEC administrative order, Release No. 34-70694.

Database Changes and Rollback Compatibility

Returning to the earlier recommendation image was possible because the query revision had not changed stored data. A different release might change the database schema or record values that an older application cannot interpret. In that case, restoring the earlier image could make the situation worse.

Suppose Baodium wants to replace a product’s category field with category_v2, whose values come from a new classification system. If the application starts reading the new field before every active writer maintains it, customers can receive missing or outdated categories. If new writers stop updating the old field too early, rolling back to old readers can produce the same problem in reverse.

The team used an expand-then-contract sequence to keep compatible versions running during the transition.

Expand and Deploy Compatible Writers

The first migration added the new column without removing the old one. PostgreSQL can add a nullable column without rewriting every existing row, but the statement still needs a table lock. If another transaction continues holding a conflicting lock, the migration may wait and block subsequent operations queued behind it.

Baodium gave this schema change a short lock-acquisition deadline.

If the lock could not be obtained promptly, the migration failed and could be rescheduled instead of waiting indefinitely behind a busy table. Large indexes were created through an appropriately planned CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY operation, which PostgreSQL requires to run outside a transaction block.

Next, a compatibility version wrote both category representations in the same local transaction. Every writer of that data had to participate, including batch imports, support tools, and recovery jobs. The team did not enable readers of category_v2 until it could verify that all active writers maintained both fields.

That compatibility version became the rollback target. An older image that wrote only category could still start successfully, but it would silently leave category_v2 outdated. Restoring such an image would violate the new reader’s assumptions.

Backfill and Verify

Existing rows needed values in the new representation. Baodium processed them in bounded batches so the backfill did not overwhelm regular transactions with additional locks, I/O, or WAL. The replicas from Chapter 7 needed to replay those changes, so the backfill rate was also limited by replication lag.

A backfill running alongside customer edits can overwrite newer data if it blindly writes a value calculated earlier. The team used guarded updates that derived the new value from the current row under appropriate transaction protection, or compared a source version before updating. Conflicting rows were retried rather than overwritten.

Verification checked whether the two representations agreed under the conversion rule. Counting non-null values would only show that the new column had been filled. It would not establish that the classification was current or correct.

Only after the backfill and writer inventory passed could the new reader path be exposed through the canary. Both representations continued to be written during the rollback window.

Contract After the Rollback Window

Removing the old column was a separate release. The team first confirmed that no deployed service, scheduled job, external consumer, or recovery procedure still depended on it. A monthly reporting job matters just as much as the serving fleet even when it does not run during the canary.

Dual writing also has limits. If the new classification accepts values that the old representation cannot express, the compatibility layer needs a documented transformation or a temporary restriction on new values. Once incompatible values have been committed, rolling back may require a forward repair rather than restoring an older binary.

API and Event Compatibility

Database columns are only one kind of shared contract. A service can also deploy a response or event format while some consumers continue using the previous version.

Adding a response field may be harmless to clients that ignore unknown fields. Other clients may reject it. Renaming a field, changing its meaning, or introducing an enum value a consumer does not recognize can break a client even when the HTTP status is unchanged.

Baodium used consumer contract tests for changes to important APIs. A tool such as Pact can express which requests a consumer sends and which response fields it requires. The provider’s build can then test the new implementation against those published expectations. Contract tests do not automatically cover clients that have never published contracts, so usage telemetry and a supported compatibility period remain important.

Events extend the overlap further. An updated consumer may read older events from a backlog, while a restored consumer may encounter events written by the candidate. Schema registries can enforce selected compatibility policies, but the team still has to account for event semantics, retention, replay, and the application effects of reprocessing. Chapter 12 develops those delivery and replay rules.

Restoration After a Candidate Has Served Traffic

A restoration rehearsal needs to include the state the candidate may already have changed. Stopping the canary and redirecting new requests to stable instances is only the first operation.

For the recommendation query, the procedure removed the candidate from new routing, allowed or canceled in-flight calls under their deadlines, and verified that connection occupancy and acquisition latency returned to the previous range. Queries already executing in PostgreSQL might continue for some time after traffic moved away.

The release record identified the earlier image digest and configuration revision, confirmed that they remained compatible with the current database, and checked that sufficient stable capacity could accept the returned traffic. In a dynamically scaled rollout, this could require starting stable instances before full recovery.

For state-changing releases, the procedure also examined durable operations accepted by the candidate. A returned image cannot reverse an emitted event, a payment authorization, or a committed order change. Those effects need the idempotent recovery and compensation procedures from Chapter 3.

The team measured two recovery intervals separately: how long it took to stop routing new requests to the candidate, and how long customer-facing service took to return to its required range. A quick routing change followed by ten minutes of database contention was still a ten-minute recovery problem for customers.

Applying Release Gates to Read Routing

The same approach applies to a change whose main risk is correctness. Suppose Baodium begins sending account-page reads to PostgreSQL replicas, as Chapter 7 described. The change may reduce primary traffic, but a replica that has not replayed the customer’s address update can return outdated information.

A canary evaluated only on latency could pass while customers saw older account state. The release plan therefore needs the read-your-writes contract, the share of reads sent to replicas, verified replay position, primary fallback rate, and the rate of responses violating the accepted freshness rule.

The cohort must include customers who actually update accounts and then read them. A random small sample of browsing requests may never exercise that sequence. The team can run targeted production-safe tests that save and immediately retrieve records, while also using real request measurements under the appropriate privacy policy.

If replica freshness fails, the controller can restore the previous read-routing rule while retaining the same application image. It must still verify that every instance has received the routing revision and that the primary can support the returned read load.

That last check links the release back to Chapter 9. A rollback that sends all replica reads to a primary without an admission limit can create a new overload. The release and its restoration path need to fit the same capacity budget.

Authorizing the Deployment Itself

So far, we have assumed that the release owner is permitted to deploy the candidate. A production change also needs an enforceable decision about who can approve it and which artifact that approval covers.

Imagine a validation service approving image A with configuration revision 17 for Baodium’s production environment. The next day, a Jenkins pipeline attempts to deploy image B using the earlier approval. If the controller checks only whether an approval exists for the change ticket, it may allow a release nobody authorized.

Another case is policy revision. Suppose the approval was issued before a rule forbidding a larger database pool became active. Whether the earlier approval can still be used depends on the organization’s execution policy. The deployment system needs a defined way to handle approval expiration, revocation, and changes to the relevant rules.

Chapter 3 introduced the difference between operation identity and permission. Reusing a deployment operation ID can retrieve an earlier evaluation, but it cannot grant the caller new authority.

Baodium’s deployment authorization bound the approval to the image digest, configuration revision, target environment, operation identity, and policy revision. It included the approver’s authority and a validity interval. The enforcement component checked these bindings and the applicable revocation policy before permitting execution.

This check had to occur in the deployment path. A Slack notification could inform the release team that a change was approved, but it could not stop a pipeline from deploying another image. The enforcement component also needed a clear ordering rule for approval revocation racing with deployment admission. A policy read performed several minutes before dispatch would leave another time-of-check/time-of-use gap.

For an operation that required current authorization, the system either made the admission decision against a sufficiently current authoritative policy record at the controlled execution boundary or refused the action until it could do so. A previously authorized deployment already in progress needed its own cancellation and audit policy. The token or change ID alone could not establish whether it was still allowed.

A PostgreSQL-backed validation module could support the initial design. More elaborate policy distribution and regional failover would be justified only by the requirements they actually served. Appendix B develops the full deployment-authorization workflow.

Summary

Baodium’s query change passed its functional tests and ran faster in an isolated benchmark. During production concurrency, it occupied database connections longer, and the rolling deployment continued because instance readiness never evaluated that cost. The revised release process used a representative canary, explicit resource limits, and observations collected before exposure increased.

The team also learned to evaluate the recovery path. Returning traffic to the previous version requires enough stable capacity and a database state that the earlier code can still understand. Feature flags can deactivate a request path, but instances must receive the updated configuration, and in-flight operations may continue after deactivation.

Those constraints become especially important when teams deploy services independently while sharing data. A schema change can leave one service ready and another unable to process its records. Chapter 11 examines that problem through Baodium’s service boundaries and the ownership decisions that determine whether independent deployments are actually possible.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & The candidate query preserves recommendation correctness and consumes no more database capacity than the release policy permits under comparable production traffic.
Condition that tests it & The canary receives representative per-instance demand and additional candidate instances increase aggregate shared-database load.
Constraint or invariant & Promotion requires comparable samples, version-specific resource evidence, and absolute customer-facing limits. Restoration must use an artifact and configuration compatible with the current database.
Evidence and uncertainty & The earlier release raised mean connection occupancy from 70 to 85 ms, which at 400 lookups/s increased average assigned connections from 28 to 34 per instance.

Still unknown: request-mix differences, shared contention at full exposure, and how quickly stable capacity returns during a late-stage abort.
Signal and evaluation window & Evaluate occupancy, acquisition latency, errors, and page outcomes across two nonoverlapping five-minute windows with sufficient canary volume. Detect missing telemetry independently.
Control and decision & Promote only after the recorded gates pass. Pause for insufficient evidence, abort on confirmed harm, and verify both route restoration and recovery of customer-facing service.
Owner and review trigger & The service owner defines the expected change and thresholds. The release owner controls exposure and aborts. Data and security owners approve compatibility and deployment authority. Review after a failed rollout or before changing the gate policy.
